pages.text: Umenopterix burkhardi was a relatively large member of the Umenocoleidae, a family of aberrant Cretaceous roach-like insects whose sclerotized forewings are easily mistaken for the elytras of unrelated beetles. Umenopterix itself is only known from the Crato Formation, a rich lagerstätte dated from the end of the Early Cretaceous and located in Northeastern Brazil.

Umenopterix, like its relatives, had likely very little sexual dimorphism between the sexes, with the ovipositor of the female being largely reduced. The surface of the elytra-like forewings seems to indicate the presence of cryptic patterning used to break the shape of the insect on a tree trunk, and it is quite likely that Umenopterix lived mostly under the bark of the plants upon which it fed.
